mcqs.question: What is the purpose of DataInputStream in Java I/O?

options.B: To read primitive Java data types from a binary input stream
options.C: To read text files line by line

mcqs.explanation: DataInputStream wraps an InputStream and provides methods like readInt(), readDouble(), readBoolean(), readUTF() to read Java primitive types from binary data. It must wrap a byte stream like FileInputStream or System.in.

mcqs.question: How do you create a DataInputStream to read from the keyboard?

options.B: new DataInputStream(System.in)

mcqs.explanation: DataInputStream dis = new DataInputStream(System.in) wraps the standard input (keyboard) stream. readInt(), readLine() (deprecated) etc. read typed data from the keyboard. Note: readLine() is deprecated; use BufferedReader.readLine() instead for text input.

mcqs.question: What is the File class used for in Java?

options.B: To represent and manipulate file and directory paths — create, delete, list, check existence

mcqs.explanation: java.io.File represents file/directory paths. Methods: exists(), createNewFile(), delete(), isDirectory(), isFile(), length(), listFiles(), mkdir(). It doesn't read/write file contents — that's done with stream classes. File is a path abstraction.

mcqs.question: Which method creates a new empty file?

options.B: file.make()

mcqs.explanation: file.createNewFile() atomically creates an empty file if it doesn't exist. Returns true if created, false if it already exists. For directories: file.mkdir() creates one directory, file.mkdirs() creates parent directories too.

mcqs.question: Which stream class reads bytes from a file?

options.B: FileInputStream

mcqs.explanation: FileInputStream reads raw bytes from a file. It's the byte stream counterpart to FileReader (characters). Example: FileInputStream fis = new FileInputStream("data.bin"); int b = fis.read();

mcqs.question: What does file.exists() return?

options.B: true if the file or directory exists at the given path

mcqs.explanation: file.exists() returns boolean — true if the file or directory exists. Common check before reading: if(file.exists()) { /* read */ } else { /* create or error */ }. Also: file.canRead(), file.canWrite(), file.canExecute().

mcqs.question: Which class writes bytes to a file?

options.B: PrintWriter

mcqs.explanation: FileOutputStream writes raw bytes to a file. Constructor: new FileOutputStream("output.bin") (overwrites) or new FileOutputStream("output.bin", true) (append). For text: use FileWriter; for primitives: use DataOutputStream wrapping FileOutputStream.

mcqs.question: What is BufferedInputStream used for?

options.B: To buffer byte input for efficiency — reduces disk I/O by reading data in chunks

mcqs.explanation: BufferedInputStream wraps an InputStream and adds an internal buffer (default 8192 bytes). Instead of reading one byte at a time from disk, it reads in chunks. Each read() returns from the buffer — much faster than unbuffered reads.

mcqs.question: What is SequenceInputStream used for?

options.B: To concatenate multiple input streams so they appear as a single sequential stream

mcqs.explanation: SequenceInputStream merges multiple InputStreams: new SequenceInputStream(s1, s2) or with an Enumeration. Reading from it reads s1 to EOF, then s2 seamlessly. Useful for merging files or reading multiple parts as one continuous stream.

mcqs.question: Which exception is thrown when a file cannot be found?

options.B: FileNotFoundException

mcqs.explanation: FileNotFoundException extends IOException. Thrown by FileInputStream, FileReader, RandomAccessFile constructors when the file doesn't exist. It's a checked exception — must be caught or declared with throws.

mcqs.question: How do you copy a file using byte streams in Java?

options.B: Read bytes from FileInputStream in a loop and write to FileOutputStream
options.D: Use Scanner to read and PrintWriter to write

mcqs.explanation: Classic copy: fis = new FileInputStream(src); fos = new FileOutputStream(dest); byte[] buf = new byte[8192]; int n; while((n=fis.read(buf)) != -1) fos.write(buf, 0, n); Java 7+: Files.copy(src.toPath(), dest.toPath()) is simpler.

mcqs.question: What is the role of BufferedOutputStream in file writing?

options.A: It adds buffering for faster writes — data accumulates in memory before being written to disk in chunks
options.B: It encrypts the output
options.C: It writes characters instead of bytes

mcqs.explanation: BufferedOutputStream wraps an OutputStream and buffers writes in memory. Each write() goes to the buffer; the buffer flushes to disk when full or when flush() is called. This reduces the number of disk writes dramatically — one large write instead of many small ones.

mcqs.question: How do you merge two files using SequenceInputStream?

options.B: Create SequenceInputStream(fis1, fis2), read from it, and write to the merged output file

mcqs.explanation: SequenceInputStream sis = new SequenceInputStream(new FileInputStream(f1), new FileInputStream(f2)); FileOutputStream fos = new FileOutputStream(merged); byte[] buf = new byte[8192]; int n; while((n=sis.read(buf)) != -1) fos.write(buf, 0, n); — reads f1 fully, then f2, writing both to merged output.

mcqs.question: What does DataInputStream.readLine() do and why is it deprecated?

options.A: Reads a line and is fine to use
options.B: Reads a line of text but is deprecated because it doesn't properly handle character encoding; use BufferedReader.readLine() instead

mcqs.explanation: DataInputStream.readLine() is deprecated because it reads bytes as ASCII without proper character encoding support — non-ASCII characters are corrupted. BufferedReader.readLine() uses the proper encoding (UTF-8, etc.) and is the correct replacement for reading text line by line.

mcqs.question: What is the correct way to read a file created by DataOutputStream?

options.B: Use DataInputStream with matching read methods (readInt for writeInt, readDouble for writeDouble)

mcqs.explanation: DataInputStream/DataOutputStream are a matched pair. If you wrote with writeInt(42), read it back with readInt(). If you wrote with writeDouble(3.14), read it with readDouble(). The order must match: if you wrote int then double, read int then double. Using BufferedReader would misinterpret the binary bytes as text.

mcqs.question: How does file.delete() work and what does it return?

options.A: Deletes the file and returns void
options.B: Deletes the file/directory; returns true if deleted successfully, false if file doesn't exist or can't be deleted

mcqs.explanation: file.delete() returns boolean — true if the file was successfully deleted, false otherwise. Common reasons for false: file doesn't exist, file is a non-empty directory (must delete contents first), file is locked by another process, insufficient permissions.

mcqs.question: What is the try-with-resources syntax for file I/O?

options.B: try { FileReader fr = new FileReader("f.txt"); }

mcqs.explanation: try(FileReader fr = new FileReader("f.txt")) { ... } — the resource (FileReader) is automatically closed when the try block ends, even if an exception occurs. Multiple resources: try(FileInputStream fis = ...; FileOutputStream fos = ...) { }. The resource must implement AutoCloseable.

mcqs.question: What is the significance of the buffer size in BufferedInputStream?

options.B: A larger buffer reads more bytes per disk access, reducing I/O calls; typical size 8KB-64KB balances memory usage and performance

mcqs.explanation: BufferedInputStream default buffer is 8192 bytes. Larger buffers (16KB-64KB) can improve throughput for large files by reducing system calls. Beyond 64KB, returns diminish — disk I/O dominates. For network streams, smaller buffers (2KB-4KB) may be better to reduce latency.

mcqs.question: How does file.length() differ from file.list()?

options.B: length() returns the file size in bytes; list() returns String[] of filenames in a directory
options.C: length() returns number of lines; list() returns file contents

mcqs.explanation: file.length() returns the file size in bytes (long). For directories, returns 0 or undefined. file.list() returns String[] of names of files/subdirectories inside a directory. For File objects representing files (not directories), list() returns null.

mcqs.question: What is the role of File.separator in cross-platform file path handling?

options.B: It provides the OS-specific path separator ('/' on Unix, '\\' on Windows) for portable path construction
options.D: It separates file names from extensions

mcqs.explanation: File.separator is '/' on Unix/Linux/macOS and '\\' on Windows. For portable paths: new File("dir" + File.separator + "file.txt"). However, Java's File constructor accepts '/' on all platforms and converts internally — so "dir/file.txt" works everywhere. File.separator is needed for string manipulation.

mcqs.question: What is the behavior of BufferedInputStream.markSupported() and when is mark/reset useful?

options.B: markSupported() returns true if the stream allows mark()/reset(); BufferedInputStream supports it, FileInputStream does not. Useful for lookahead parsing

mcqs.explanation: mark(readLimit) saves the current position; reset() seeks back to it. BufferedInputStream supports this because it buffers data — it can re-read from the buffer. FileInputStream doesn't support mark/reset because it reads from disk (can't rewind). Useful for parsing: peek ahead to identify format, then reset to parse properly.

mcqs.question: Why is DataInputStream.readInt() endian-dependent, and how does Java's default compare to network byte order?

options.A: Java uses little-endian; network uses big-endian
options.B: Java DataInputStream uses big-endian (network byte order) by default, matching the internet protocol standard
options.C: Java doesn't care about byte order
options.D: DataInputStream uses the OS default byte order

mcqs.explanation: DataInputStream.readInt() reads 4 bytes in big-endian order (most significant byte first). This matches network byte order (RFC 1700) and Java's internal representation. Intel x86 CPUs are little-endian, so reading x86-written binary files with DataInputStream requires byte-swapping. ByteBuffer with ByteOrder.LITTLE_ENDIAN handles this.

mcqs.question: What is the risk of not closing a FileOutputStream before the program exits?

options.B: Buffered data may be lost; on some OSes the file remains locked; data corruption is possible if the file is reopened before the OS flushes

mcqs.explanation: If using BufferedOutputStream wrapping FileOutputStream, unflushed data stays in the buffer and is lost on JVM exit. On Windows, unclosed files may be locked, preventing other programs from accessing them. The JVM may close files on exit, but this is unreliable — always close streams explicitly or use try-with-resources.

mcqs.question: What happens when SequenceInputStream reaches EOF of the first stream?

options.B: Automatically switches to the next stream in the sequence without any visible change — read() returns the first byte of the next stream

mcqs.explanation: SequenceInputStream transparently switches from stream 1 to stream 2 when stream 1 reaches EOF. The caller sees a continuous stream of bytes. read() returns -1 only when ALL streams in the sequence are exhausted. This makes merging multiple files transparent to the reading code.

mcqs.question: In the demonstration, what is the purpose of using DataOutputStream to write student records?

options.A: To store records as human-readable text
options.B: To write each field (name, roll, marks) as typed binary data (writeUTF for name, writeInt for roll, writeDouble for marks) for compact storage

mcqs.explanation: DataOutputStream writes typed binary data: writeUTF(name), writeInt(rollNo), writeDouble(marks). This is compact (4 bytes for int vs variable-length text), fast to read back with DataInputStream (no parsing needed), but not human-readable. Trade-off: efficiency vs readability.

mcqs.question: What is the difference between file.canWrite() returning true and actually being able to write to the file?

options.B: canWrite() checks the OS permission bits but doesn't guarantee write success — the file could be locked by another process, disk could be full, or filesystem read-only
options.D: canWrite() always returns true on Windows

mcqs.explanation: canWrite() checks the Java SecurityManager and OS file permission bits. However, actual write may fail due to: file locked by another process (Windows), read-only filesystem mount, disk full, network share permissions. Always handle IOException on write, even if canWrite() returns true.

mcqs.question: How does the JVM handle a file path on different operating systems when using the File class?

options.B: Java normalizes path separators — '/' works on all platforms; File internally converts to the OS-specific separator

mcqs.explanation: new File("dir/subdir/file.txt") works on all platforms. Java internally converts '/' to the OS separator ('\' on Windows). File.getAbsolutePath(), getCanonicalPath() return OS-specific paths. For maximum portability, always use '/' in Java paths — no need for File.separator in most cases.

mcqs.question: What is a 'file lock' and how does it differ between RandomAccessFile and FileChannel?

options.A: File locking is automatic in both
options.B: RandomAccessFile has no built-in locking; FileChannel provides tryLock()/lock() for OS-level exclusive or shared file locks, enabling cross-process coordination

mcqs.explanation: RandomAccessFile has no lock mechanism — multiple processes can access the same file concurrently with no coordination. FileChannel.tryLock() / lock() use OS-level file locking (advisory on Unix, mandatory on Windows) to coordinate access across processes. FileLock is released when the channel closes or the JVM exits.

mcqs.question: What is the correct idiom for reading a binary file with a specific format (e.g., header then records) using DataInputStream?

options.B: Read header fields with matching types (readInt for magic number, readShort for version), then loop reading records (readUTF for name, readInt for value) until EOF
options.C: Read the entire file as bytes and parse manually

mcqs.explanation: For binary formats: read the header (e.g., magic = dis.readInt(); version = dis.readShort()), then loop: while(true) { try { String name = dis.readUTF(); int value = dis.readInt(); } catch(EOFException e) { break; } }. EOFException signals end of records. The read order must exactly match the write order.

mcqs.question: What is the performance implication of using DataInputStream.readInt() vs reading a byte[] and extracting ints manually with bit shifting?

options.B: DataInputStream.readInt() internally reads 4 bytes and assembles the int with bit shifting — it's essentially the same as manual extraction but more readable and handles EOF correctly
options.C: Manual bit shifting is always faster

mcqs.explanation: DataInputStream.readInt() reads 4 bytes and combines them: (b0<<24) | (b1<<16) | (b2<<8) | b3 — big-endian assembly. Manual extraction with ByteBuffer.wrap(buf).getInt() can be faster for bulk reads (ByteBuffer uses direct memory and can use native byte order). For single reads, DataInputStream is fine; for bulk reads, ByteBuffer is more efficient.
